subject: typescript
title: Functions
description: Parameter and return annotations, optional and default parameters, void vs never.

content.title: Definition
content.body: A function type describes what goes in and what comes out. Parameters are checked by position, and the return type is usually better left to inference — except on exported API, where an explicit return type stops a refactor from silently widening it.

content.title: Optional vs default
content.body: An optional parameter may be omitted and is then undefined. A default parameter may also be omitted but never is undefined inside the body.

content.title: Watch out
content.body: void means "ignore whatever is returned", not "returns nothing". never means the function cannot return at all — it throws or loops forever.

exercises.question: What is the inferred return type?
exercises.explanation: Multiplying two numbers yields a number, so TypeScript infers it without an annotation.

exercises.question: When is never the right return type?

answers.text: When the return value should be ignored
When the function returns nothing useful
When the function cannot return normally — it always throws or never terminates

exercises.explanation: void covers "returns nothing useful". never is the empty type: no value inhabits it, so the function has no normal exit.

exercises.question: Which line does the compiler reject?

answers.text: Line 1 — a required parameter cannot follow an optional one
Line 4 — the call passes too many arguments

exercises.explanation: Optional parameters must come last, otherwise a caller could not skip them. Swap the order or give value a default.

exercises.question: Complete the alias describing a function that takes a number and returns a string.
exercises.explanation: A function type uses => for its return type. A colon is used inside interfaces and object type literals for method shorthand.

exercises.question: A parameter with a default value still has undefined in its type inside the function body.
exercises.explanation: The default is applied before the body runs, so the parameter's type inside the body excludes undefined — unlike an optional parameter.

exercises.question: What is the type of values?
exercises.explanation: A rest parameter collects the remaining arguments into a real array, so it is annotated as an array type.

exercises.question: Complete the annotation for an async function resolving to a User.
exercises.explanation: An async function always returns a promise, so its annotated return type has to be Promise<T>.

exercises.question: TypeScript · functions
exercises.back: Function overloads — callers see only the signatures, never the implementation one
exercises.explanation: The implementation signature must be compatible with every overload but is not itself callable from outside.

exercises.question: Why may a callback of type (a: number) => void be passed where (a: number, b: number) => void is expected?

answers.text: Because void return types disable parameter checks
It may not — the arities must match exactly
A function that ignores trailing parameters is always safe to call with more arguments
TypeScript pads the missing parameter with undefined

exercises.explanation: Fewer parameters is always compatible: the extra arguments are simply unused. This is why arr.map(n => n * 2) type-checks despite map passing three arguments.

exercises.question: Why does the arrow version work and the other one not?

answers.text: An arrow function captures this from the class instance; a detached method loses it
Methods cannot be destructured in TypeScript

exercises.explanation: Passing a method as a callback is the usual way this goes wrong. Arrow properties cost one closure per instance, which is the trade.

exercises.question: Why annotate the return type of an exported function even though inference works?

answers.text: It stops a refactor silently widening the public contract, and keeps errors at the definition
Inference does not work across modules
It is required by strict mode
It makes the build faster at runtime

exercises.explanation: Without it, returning null from a new branch changes every consumer's type instead of failing where the change was made.

exercises.question: Complete the signature so callers narrow after the check.
exercises.explanation: A type predicate is a promise the compiler takes at face value, so the body has to actually test what it claims.

exercises.question: `callback?.()` calls the function only when callback is neither null nor undefined.
exercises.explanation: It short-circuits to undefined otherwise. Note that it does not guard against callback being a non-callable value of another type.

exercises.question: Which line makes the error disappear silently?

answers.text: Line 2 — await is not allowed there
Line 1 — Promise<void> is not a valid return type
Line 6 — the promise is not awaited, so a rejection becomes an unhandled rejection

exercises.explanation: The compiler allows it; the no-floating-promises lint rule is what catches it. Either await it or mark the intent with void save().

exercises.question: What does a helper with the signature `(value: never) => never` buy you in a switch default?

answers.text: A compile error the moment a new union member is not handled
A runtime exception for unknown values
Automatic handling of the new case

exercises.explanation: If every case is handled, the value is narrowed to never and the call type-checks. Add a member and it stops compiling — which is the point.
